toc.title: You don't have to, but it will likely happen
When crying doesn't seem to help
Observing is the starting point, not the goal

blocks.p: I recently answered a question about emotional regulation and crying: do we allow, or do we do? Are we allowing the process to happen, or making ourselves do something? I made the case that it's probably a balance of both, but I lean more toward allowing. Based on the Polyvagal Theory teachings, at least the way I understand them, our bodies have a natural predisposition toward homeostasis and self-regulation. The body already wants to regulate. Our conscious selves need to allow it to happen.
Then one listener left a comment that really gripped my attention. Here's how it started:

q: Hi, I'm new. Topic gripping. Must we permit, and welcome by the way, must we permit sadness to overwhelm unto weeping in order to heal?

blocks.p: The way I read it: do we have to permit sadness to the point where it's so overwhelming that it turns into weeping, in order to heal? Let's work through it.

blocks.h: You don't have to, but it will likely happen

blocks.p: I'm reluctant to say we have to do anything when it comes to self-regulation and trauma recovery. I don't want to tell you what your path is. There are common milestones on the journey that you'll likely find yourself at, but I'm very reluctant to say one must do this or that.

According to the Polyvagal Theory, there are some general things that probably must happen. We have to build the strength of our safety state, for example. But must someone tell their trauma story? Must someone think of themselves in terms of having parts, or an ego, or a shadow? Some of this is subjective. It's up to you.

Crying is very likely going to be part of the trauma recovery journey. Sadness and overwhelm are likely to be part of it too. So do you need to feel these things so intensely that you cry? The way I do things as a therapist, and the way I teach self-regulation: no, you don't have to. But it likely will happen.

This comes in once you've built your safety state and start looking inward, going from noticing just the emotion to what lies underneath it. Maybe you can notice the emotion of sadness. That's great. But underneath the sadness are other things: bodily sensations and impulses.
I group emotions and cognitions, our thoughts, together. They hang out on the same layer, and I'd call them tertiary to the real issue. They come after sensations and impulses.

Sensations are what you feel. They're how you know you have an emotion. You know you have sadness because you feel heaviness. You feel like you're in a dark void. You feel little to no energy, no motivation. Those are sensations that are the experience of having an emotion like sadness. In a fight state, people often describe a racing heart, or heat in their chest.
Impulses come along with emotions and their underlying sensations, and they tell us what to do with them.
So if you can notice you have sadness, great. Here's how to go further.

ol: Anchor in safety. This is the start of what I call the AWE method: allow, witness, experience. You anchor in safety first.
Allow. Allow yourself to feel what you feel. Maybe you can say, "I feel sadness."

Witness. Shift into a third-party observer mode to identify where the sadness lives in your body. You're zooming out and getting into more of a researcher mindset. You're not delving directly into what it feels like yet. You're noticing where it lives in your body.

Experience. Then zoom in, more specifically, to where that emotion lives in your body, and describe what it's like to have it there. If that's difficult, try putting words to it. Give it a temperature, a size, a shape, a color. Describe what it's like to have that emotion. Underneath your sadness might be heaviness. It might feel like you're curled up and alone in a dark room with one light hanging above you, on but flickering. That might be the image of what it feels like to be you when you're sad. It might feel like rejection. Memories might come along with it. Sometimes sadness just feels like it's draping on us, and that's valid too.

Let an impulse arise. If you can tap into that layer of your sadness, mindfully and compassionately, which is not easy, an impulse may come up from it. Oftentimes, and this is good, that's going to be crying.

blocks.p: So do we have to cry in order to heal? I don't want to say you have to, but it will likely happen, especially if you're coming from a dorsal vagal shutdown state or a freeze state. That returning or discharging sympathetic energy is likely to come back, or release, as crying. Especially, I think, from freeze.
You don't need to force yourself to cry in order to heal. But when and if you feel the impulse to cry, allowing it will help healing move along.

blocks.h: When crying doesn't seem to help

blocks.p: Some people cry a ton and feel like they can't get any further down their trauma recovery journey. That's likely because while they're crying, they're judging themselves. They're telling themselves they're weak. They're hiding it, keeping it a secret, crying in isolation on the bathroom floor, or in their room, in the closet, in the dark. They're not compassionately, mindfully experiencing the bodily sensations and the release that can come along with crying.
Or maybe you just have a ton of crying to do, and you're not there yet. That's okay.

The listener went on to ask whether there's a conflict with meditation here, and wrote that "describe again, which equals observe notice sensations, therefore equals focus and awareness," and that "actively describing would accomplish that presence. This is meditating, which I do when these sensations arrive."
I don't see a conflict, and I agree. I would call this meditating. You can meditate when these sensations arrive, or you can use this process to get to the underlying sensations.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.h: Observing is the starting point, not the goal

blocks.p: Here's where we part ways a bit. The listener described "the act of tuning awareness onto sensation, then broaden observation, alert, expand intelligent as possible, attentive third party observation," and said that "third party observation permits the stoic to watch. This disempowers negative sensations fast."

For me, third-party observation is often the starting point. If you're well practiced, you might not need it. It's the zooming out that helps you find where an emotion lives. It might be a first step.

But we don't want to disempower these sensations. We want to welcome them, compassionately and mindfully. If you've developed your safety state enough, you'll be able to welcome what it's like to have these more negative emotions, with compassion and curiosity, and experience them. They're not really negative, but we'll frame it that way. And if you can do that from your safety state, they won't be experienced as negative. They'll be turned into something else.

As long as the safety state is active, it repurposes the defensive activation. The fight energy you might feel when dysregulated turns into more of an empowerment when your safety state is active. In my experience, and from what I see with my clients, the safety state doesn't produce this disempowering effect on negative sensations. It doesn't blunt them, and it doesn't create a third-party, stoic, objective distance. Instead, it makes you a direct experiencer of what's happening within you.
The listener added: "Mine are powerful and abruptly come and go due to my method of meditation. I reckon I feel better for long use of this trick."

We'd disagree there as well. These aren't tricks. What I practice myself and teach is how to feel what it's like to be you, in all regards. That includes what it feels like to be you in safety, and what it's like to be you with these more typically uncomfortable emotions, sensations, and impulses. It's how to be with yourself consciously, mindfully, and compassionately, not how to trick yourself into distancing, numbing, or cutting off defensive activation.

I think a lot of times we treat meditation as a third-party, objective thing, as if we're distancing ourselves from our present moment experience and becoming watchers of our cognitions floating in and out. I don't personally look at it that way, and I don't teach it that way. That might be the first step. But it's a portal, a window into a deeper experience of yourself.

So I don't want my clients and students to use tricks or hacks to diminish defensive activation. Ultimately, eventually, we want to welcome it, with genuine compassion and curiosity. You may not be there right now, and that's totally fine. It's not easy and it's not fast. It's a process that constantly unfolds, with continuous practice: building your safety state, and then eventually feeling defensive activation and those more negative experiences.
The listener wrapped up with a final question: "Can individual healing methods be varied as needed, or is it that all who will be healed shall first endure bitter weeping?"

The word "endure" strikes me. I don't know this person, and I have no idea if they meant it this way. But crying is not a punishment. It's not an affliction. It's not a virus. It's your self, your body, releasing flight, fight, or freeze activation it's probably been holding on to, potentially for quite a while, and the pain and sadness it's been holding on to. It's lovingly and compassionately feeling it yourself, and hopefully releasing it.

So I would hope it's a different experience than enduring. For many of us, it's not, at least not yet. That's okay. That's valid, and normal. But ideally, eventually, we get to the place where it is a different experience. Crying can come along with appreciation. It can come with gratitude. It can come with compassion.

Can individual healing methods be varied? Yes, of course. There's no one right way to do this. There are probably many different things that could be helpful for you. There are tons of therapeutic modalities I'm not trained in and have no interest in using, but for you, whatever it is might be the bee's knees, and I'm happy for you. All of this is individualized.

But along the journey, no matter what vehicle you take to get there, there are typical milestones and landmarks you might hit. Crying might be one of them. Telling your trauma narrative might be one of them.
So I do think crying, releasing, is likely going to be part of pretty much any trauma recovery journey. Would I say it must happen? I won't go that far. But it's likely.

And crying from dysregulation, from detachment, from a lack of self-compassion is different from crying from safety, from curiosity, from releasing whatever is inside of you and then feeling gratitude for the process. It's a much different experience.
